name: Aaron Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for agreeing to talk. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, 27. I live with my girlfriend Chloe in a rented place on Hill Street, she's a teaching assistant at the primary school. I work at Oakridge Furniture, they make kitchen cabinet doors and drawer fronts. I've been there about nine months, before that I was labouring on building sites.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the edge-bander mostly, which glues a thin strip onto the raw edge of each board so it looks finished, and some days I help load the CNC router, which cuts the doors out of big sheets from a program. I stack, check for chipped edges and wrap the doors for dispatch. I'm still not great at reading the cutting lists and Tony, the lead hand, catches my mistakes, but I'm getting there. My dad was a joiner for thirty years, so I grew up around wood, and I like the smell of it, even if MDF dust is a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, good old-fashioned work still counts. Dad would be pleased, he never trusted any of it. I'd probably say it at the dinner table more than anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and keep learning, which is what I want. I've used the AI a couple of times, like to help me word an email to the landlord about the damp, and it was fine. But it's not going to cut a cabinet door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Oakridge and try to get moved onto the router properly, which pays a bit more. On weekends I'd keep helping Dad with his odd jobs, which brings in maybe eighty a month. We'd try to put a bit by, but honestly at the moment there's nothing left by the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Settled. The usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the weekend jobs with your dad.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's got a bad back now, so he can't do the heavy lifting, but he still gets calls from people who want a shelf put up or a door rehung. I do the lifting and he tells me what I'm doing wrong. Last Saturday we hung four doors for an old lady on Mill Lane and she gave us tea and a fruit cake as well as the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there robots at Oakridge already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a robot arm that loads the big sheets onto the router on Line A, they put it in before I started. The guy who used to do that went onto the paint line. Tony says if it does well they'll put one on Line B, which is where I am.

S0.say: He'd say good old-fashioned work still counts and that his father, who never trusted AI, would be pleased. He'd mostly say it at the dinner table.
S0.think: He thinks he keeps his job and keeps learning, which is what he wants. He's used AI a couple of times for emails, but doesn't see it cutting a cabinet door.
S0.do: Carries on at the furniture factory aiming to move onto the router for a bit more pay. Keeps helping his father with weekend odd jobs for about eighty a month and tries, so far without success, to save.
S0.quote: Last Saturday we hung four doors for an old lady on Mill Lane and she gave us tea and a fruit cake as well as the money.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron's life is bound up with his father's trade and their weekend jobs together. He's an occasional AI user but sees no threat from software. The robot loader on Line A is a quiet signal he notes but doesn't dwell on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's up to people to get a proper trade, and businesses should take on apprentices instead of complaining about skills. I'm not one for big government schemes, but apprenticeships work, my dad's proof of that. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job on the edge-bander is pretty easy to automate, it's mostly feeding and stacking. If the robot on Line A works out, Line B's next, and I'm the newest. I'd want to have a trade in my hands before that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for a bit to see which trades are holding up. My friend Jamie started an electrician's apprenticeship last year, so if he's doing well by spring, I'd apply for the same scheme. The wage is lower, so Chloe and I might have to move in with my parents for a couple of years, which my mum would love and Chloe would put up with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit uneasy. But I'd feel like I had a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your parents to afford an apprenticeship. How would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not ideal at 28. But that's what family's for, isn't it, my dad lived with his uncle when he did his apprenticeship. I'd pay my way, do the garden, fix things. I'd rather do that than take money from the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch Jamie first. What would make you decide it's working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he's getting proper work on sites and not just sweeping up, and if his boss is keeping him on. Jamie doesn't sugarcoat things, he'll tell me if it's no good. If he says go for it, I go for it.

S1.say: He'd say people need to get a proper trade and businesses should take on apprentices rather than complain about skills. He's not keen on big government schemes but believes apprenticeships work, with his father as proof.
S1.think: Privately he sees his edge-bander work as easy to automate and knows his line is likely next after the robot on Line A. He wants a trade in hand before that happens.
S1.do: Watches how a friend's electrician apprenticeship goes and applies for the same scheme by spring if it's working. Plans to move in with his parents with his girlfriend to manage on an apprentice wage.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, but sees a way through.
S1.quote: My dad lived with his uncle when he did his apprenticeship. I'd pay my way, do the garden, fix things.
S1.fieldNote: His answer is a trade and family support, firmly not government help. He'll move once a friend he trusts proves the path. Moving back home is framed as family tradition, not failure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's been rushed by people who've never done a day's work with their hands. I'd say families and communities need to pull together, because I don't trust the government to sort it. I'd probably get a bit heated about it at Dad's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's the end of Oakridge for me, and maybe the end of the electrician idea too. If robots can wire a house, what's the point of a four-year apprenticeship? Two years isn't even long enough to finish one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away, no going out, cancel the gym, sell my old car and use Chloe's. I'd do as many weekend jobs with Dad as I could find, while people still want a person to come round. When Oakridge let me go, we'd move in with my parents and I'd take any work going, labouring, removals, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also angry. Like someone moved the goalposts while I was running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Oakridge would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tony. He's 55, he's been there since school, he knows every machine in that place. He'd be the last to go but he'd have the furthest to fall. He's got a mortgage and a wife who's not well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take any work. Would you also take government support, if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was that or Chloe going without, yes. I'd hate it though. My dad has never signed a form for money in his life, and I'd feel like I'd let him down.

S2.say: He'd say it was rushed by people who've never worked with their hands and that families and communities must pull together, since he doesn't trust government to sort it.
S2.think: He thinks it ends both his factory job and his electrician plan, since two years isn't enough to finish an apprenticeship and robots could wire houses anyway.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard, cancels the gym and sells his car to share his girlfriend's. Takes every weekend job with his father he can, and after losing the factory job moves in with his parents and takes any work, such as labouring or removals.
S2.feel: Scared and angry, like the goalposts moved mid-run.
S2.quote: If robots can wire a house, what's the point of a four-year apprenticeship? Two years isn't even long enough to finish one.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture knocks out his main plan, the apprenticeship, which is what hurts most. He'd accept government help only if his partner would otherwise go without, and would feel he'd let his father down. His blame is aimed at people who've never done manual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a few years, so get a trade, get skills, look after your own. I'd tell younger guys at work to sign up for an apprenticeship now. I'd say businesses should step up and train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32. I could finish an apprenticeship by then, just about, and get a year or two of proper electrician's wages before it lands. I don't know if that's enough, but it's better than being on the edge-bander when the robot comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see how Jamie's going, and then I'd start the apprenticeship by next autumn. We'd move in with my parents to make the wage work and try to save a bit each month, maybe forty. I'd keep the weekend jobs with Dad going for extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I was doing the right thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything with Chloe, like marriage or children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably hold off on kids. I'd want to be qualified first, with my own place, before we start. Chloe's 26, so we've got a bit of time, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell younger workers to sign up for an apprenticeship. Is that advice you'd follow yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, I'd be doing it, so yes. But I'd still wait to see Jamie get on first. Maybe that's a bit cautious, but I've got no money to waste on the wrong thing.

S3.say: He'd say there are a few years, so people should get a trade and look after their own, urging younger co-workers to start apprenticeships. Businesses, he'd add, should step up and train people.
S3.think: He thinks he could just finish an apprenticeship by 32 and earn electrician's wages for a year or two before AGI lands. He's unsure that's enough but sees it as better than staying on the edge-bander.
S3.do: Waits a few months to see how his friend is doing, then starts an electrician apprenticeship by next autumn. Moves in with his parents to manage on the wage, saves about forty a month and keeps doing weekend jobs with his father.
S3.feel: Worried, but sure he's doing the right thing.
S3.quote: Maybe that's a bit cautious, but I've got no money to waste on the wrong thing.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes his trade plan just about workable, and he commits to it after a short wait. He'd hold off on children until qualified. His caution comes from having no money to absorb a wrong move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to learn a proper trade, so there's no excuse. I'd say it to the younger ones at work, and to anyone at Dad's who'll listen. Families should be helping their kids get skills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think I'd be alright for most of it. I'd be qualified and working as an electrician for five or six years before it lands, maybe even running jobs. The end still bothers me, but I'd have savings and a trade by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see how Jamie gets on through the next year, then start the apprenticeship. I'd keep doing weekends with Dad to pay my way. Once I'm qualified I'd save properly, a couple of hundred a month, so we can buy a small place before it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families should help their kids get skills. What would you want for your own kids, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to know how to work with their hands and how to look after people, because whatever happens, people still need people. And I'd want them close to family. That's what's carried my family through everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make ten years feel too short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I waited too long, I suppose. If I spent three years watching Jamie and not starting. I'd have to give myself a deadline, like, if I haven't started by next September, I'm being a coward.

S4.say: He'd say ten years leaves no excuse not to learn a proper trade and that families should help their children gain skills now.
S4.think: He expects to be fine for most of the decade, qualified and working as an electrician for five or six years before AGI arrives. The end point still bothers him, but he'd have savings and a trade.
S4.do: Watches his friend's progress for a year, then starts the apprenticeship while keeping weekend work with his father. Once qualified, saves a couple of hundred a month aiming to buy a small home before AGI arrives.
S4.feel: Mostly okay, uneasy at the edges.
S4.quote: If I haven't started by next September, I'm being a coward.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his traditional path of trade and family looks solid to him. He catches the risk in his own waiting and sets himself a deadline. His hopes for future children centre on hands-on skills, caring and family ties.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to get a trade, and my plan's gone before it starts. What would help is businesses keeping people on and paying for proper apprenticeships, and families and churches looking out for each other. Not some government cheque that tells you to stay home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my dad. He did thirty years with his hands and now his back's gone, and I'm the one carrying the doors for him. If the robots take the factory work and the trades, what am I meant to pass on to my own kids?

headlineQuote: If the robots take the factory work and the trades, what am I meant to pass on to my own kids?
portrait: Aaron Rossi is a 27-year-old edge-bander operator at a kitchen cabinet factory, son of a joiner, who spends weekends doing odd jobs alongside his father. He's used AI only a few times and believes in trades, apprenticeships and family over government schemes. In steady change he plans an electrician's apprenticeship, waiting first to see how a friend gets on, and would move in with his parents to afford it. Fast AGI wipes out that plan and leaves him scared and angry, while five or ten years make it workable. He worries most about what skills he can pass on to children he doesn't have yet.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to get a trade and his plan is gone before it starts.
whatWouldHelp: Businesses keeping people on and paying for proper apprenticeships, with families and churches looking out for each other rather than a government cheque.
